summary: Psalm 112 begins with praise and describes the blessed life of a person who fears Yahweh and delights in his commandments. The poem moves from family and household stability to generosity, courage under bad news, and a final contrast with the wicked whose desire fails.
whyItMatters: This psalm stands in Book V of Psalms as wisdom-shaped praise: it portrays the upright life as reverent, generous, steady, and remembered. It also echoes the Psalter's larger concern that righteousness and wickedness lead in different directions.

context.author: Anonymous within the psalm itself; Psalms as a book is a many-writer anthology formed over time.
context.audience: Israel's worshiping and instructed community, and later Jewish and Christian communities who received Psalms for prayer and instruction.
context.date: Individual psalms come from different periods, and assigning one date to the whole Psalter would be misleading.
context.setting: Book V of Psalms, a section concerned with return, Torah, pilgrimage, thanksgiving, and praise.
context.literaryForm: Compressed Hebrew poetry. Psalm 112 is an alphabetic acrostic in Hebrew, though that structure is not visible in ordinary English translation.

outline.heading: Praise and the Reverent Life
outline.note: The psalm opens with praise and names the blessed person as one who fears Yahweh and delights in his commandments.

outline.heading: Blessing in Household and Legacy
outline.note: The upright person's offspring, house, wealth, and enduring righteousness are described as blessed.

outline.heading: Light and Gracious Conduct
outline.note: The upright receive light in darkness and are marked by graciousness, mercy, lending, and fair dealing.

outline.heading: Steadiness Without Fear
outline.note: The righteous person is not shaken, is remembered, and remains steadfast even when facing evil news and adversaries.

outline.heading: Generosity and Honor
outline.note: The righteous person gives to the poor, and the verse repeats that his righteousness endures forever.

outline.heading: The Wicked See and Perish
outline.note: The psalm ends by contrasting the wicked person's grief, anger, and fading desire with the honored righteous person.

keyVerses.text: Praise Yah! Blessed is the man who fears Yahweh, who delights greatly in his commandments.
keyVerses.why: This verse gives the psalm's starting point: praise, reverence for Yahweh, and delight in his commandments.

keyVerses.text: Light dawns in the darkness for the upright, gracious, merciful, and righteous.
keyVerses.why: This anchors the psalm's picture of the upright person as one who meets darkness without being defined by it.

keyVerses.text: He will not be afraid of evil news. His heart is steadfast, trusting in Yahweh.
keyVerses.why: This verse names the inner steadiness that the psalm associates with trust in Yahweh.

keyVerses.text: He has dispersed, he has given to the poor. His righteousness endures forever. His horn will be exalted with honor.
keyVerses.why: This verse gathers the psalm's emphasis on generosity, lasting righteousness, and public honor.

themes: fear of Yahweh and delight in commandments
the blessed generation of the upright
the failed desire of the wicked

questions.question: What does this psalm mean by “Blessed”?
questions.answer: In verse 1, “Blessed” describes the life of the person who fears Yahweh and delights in his commandments. The rest of the psalm fills out that blessedness through family, household provision, righteousness, generosity, courage, and lasting remembrance.

questions.question: Does “fears Yahweh” mean being terrified of God?
questions.answer: The verse pairs fearing Yahweh with delighting greatly in his commandments, so the phrase points to reverent loyalty rather than panic. The psalm describes this fear by its visible fruit: uprightness, mercy, generosity, and trust.

questions.question: Is this psalm promising that righteous people will always be wealthy?
questions.answer: Verse 3 says, “Wealth and riches are in his house,” but the psalm is poetic wisdom, not a ledger of every faithful person's experience. The wider shape of Psalms includes both confident statements like this and prayers from people who suffer, so readers should not flatten the line into a guarantee that removes hardship.

questions.question: Why does verse 4 say light dawns “in the darkness”?
questions.answer: The verse does not deny darkness; it says light dawns there for the upright. In this chapter, that light is connected with a character described as gracious, merciful, and righteous, and with a heart that remains steady when evil news comes.

questions.question: What kind of generosity does the psalm describe?
questions.answer: The psalm speaks of a person who “deals graciously and lends” and who “has given to the poor.” It presents generosity not as a passing mood but as part of the righteous person's settled way of life.

questions.question: What does “He will maintain his cause in judgment” mean here?
questions.answer: Verse 5 connects gracious dealing and lending with being able to stand in judgment. The line suggests that the person's conduct can bear examination, but the psalm does not give a court scene or specify the exact setting.

questions.question: Why does the psalm repeat that righteousness “endures forever”?
questions.answer: The phrase appears in verses 3 and 9, framing both the person's household and the person's generosity. The repetition makes lasting righteousness one of the chapter's central claims, especially when contrasted with the wicked person's desire that perishes in verse 10.

questions.question: What is meant by “His horn will be exalted with honor”?
questions.answer: In verse 9, “horn” is an image attached to honor and exaltation. The psalm does not pause to explain the image, but in this line it marks the public lifting up of the generous righteous person.

questions.question: Why does the wicked person react with grief and gnashing teeth?
questions.answer: Verse 10 shows the wicked seeing the honor of the righteous and being grieved. The verse pictures anger and collapse, ending with “The desire of the wicked will perish,” so the contrast is between enduring righteousness and frustrated wicked desire.

glossary.def: The psalm's opening call to praise, using a shortened form of Yahweh's name.
A word for the flourishing condition of the person described in the psalm, beginning with reverence for Yahweh and delight in his commandments.
The psalm's term for the righteous person whose life is marked by mercy, generosity, steadiness, and trust.
Bad or threatening news that does not make the righteous person's heart collapse in fear.
An image in verse 9 for honor being lifted up or exalted.
